agents.name: Eribulin
agents.explanation: Eribulin blocks the growth of microtubules, the small structures a cell needs to divide. It can slow liposarcoma growth but can also affect blood production and nerves.
agents.watch: Report fever or sudden illness immediately. Report numbness, weakness or difficulty walking before another dose; palpitations, fainting or a blistering rash need urgent assessment.
risks: Low blood counts, serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding
Numbness, tingling, pain or weakness from nerve injury, sometimes lasting
Fatigue, hair loss, nausea, vomiting, mouth soreness, diarrhoea or constipation
Changes in the heart electrical recovery interval (QT), especially with other risk factors or interacting medicines
Rare severe blistering or peeling skin reactions; allergic reactions; fertility and pregnancy harm
visual: Blood counts and nerves need review

anatomy: Report mouth ulcers, soreness or trouble drinking early. Use the prescribed mouth-care and anti-sickness plan.
Palpitations or fainting need urgent assessment. The team checks heart-rhythm risks and interacting medicines.
Blood tests detect liver effects. Yellow eyes, dark urine or new significant upper abdominal pain needs prompt assessment.
Kidney tests help the team choose safe treatment. Report reduced urine or difficulty drinking promptly.
Low counts can cause infection, anaemia or bleeding. Fever, shaking chills or sudden illness needs immediate oncology contact.
Report persistent diarrhoea or constipation, severe pain, abdominal swelling or inability to drink.
Hair loss and rash may occur. Blistering or peeling skin or sores involving the eyes or mouth need urgent assessment.
Report numbness, tingling or weakness before the next dose. Nerve effects may affect walking or hand tasks and can persist.

monitoring_test_details.label: Full blood count
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Check infection, anaemia and bleeding risks before each planned dose.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and before day 1 and day 8 treatment decisions. Initial eligibility differs from later treatment-day withholding criteria.

monitoring_test_details.label: Kidney and liver tests
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Guide medicine handling and dose review.
monitoring_test_details.timing: At baseline and at cycle start; repeat sooner for symptoms, abnormal results or clinical concerns.

monitoring_test_details.label: Nerve function
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Detect sensory or motor injury affecting daily tasks.
monitoring_test_details.timing: Before further doses and whenever numbness, tingling, weakness or difficulty walking changes.

monitoring_test_details.label: Heart rhythm and electrolytes
monitoring_test_details.purpose: Identify electrical-rhythm risk and correct contributing abnormalities.
monitoring_test_details.timing: An electrocardiogram (heart tracing) and relevant electrolyte tests are used when cardiac disease, slow heart rate, interacting medicines or other rhythm risks indicate them. There is no universal fixed heart-test calendar.

monitoring_test_details.purpose: Assess benefit separately from safety blood tests.
monitoring_test_details.timing: The specialist sets scan and clinical-review timing for the tumour type, treatment aim and symptoms.

support.title: Preparation and support medicines
support.text: Bring all medicines and report numbness, weakness, constipation, infection or fainting before treatment. Review medicines that affect heart rhythm. Arrange written contraception instructions and avoid breastfeeding during treatment. This is a low nausea/vomiting-risk regimen. Agree individual anti-sickness and bowel support; National Cancer Control Programme lists no usual separate premedication. White-cell growth-factor support may be chosen for severe neutropenia, but there is no universal routine course.

support.title: Access and practical care
support.text: The team chooses appropriate intravenous access and explains its care. Report pain, burning, redness or swelling during treatment immediately. If a port or peripherally inserted central catheter is used, confirm dressing, flushing, infection precautions and eventual removal arrangements.

support.title: Fertility and pregnancy precautions
support.text: Discuss fertility preservation before treatment. Avoid pregnancy and obtain written contraception and breastfeeding instructions for every medicine, including how long precautions continue after the last dose. Do not assume all drugs have the same waiting period. Contact oncology promptly if pregnancy is possible. The readable current manufacturer information specifies highly effective contraception for women during treatment and for 7 months afterwards, and effective contraception for men with partners who could become pregnant during treatment and for 4 months afterwards. Confirm the supplied product and personal plan.

support.title: Your wider treatment plan
support.text: A specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team reviews the exact pathology, disease extent, prior treatment and your priorities. Surgery or radiotherapy can have a separate role in selected situations. Symptom control, rehabilitation and palliative care can accompany systemic treatment; they are not restricted to the end of life.

support.title: Driving and daily tasks
support.text: Do not drive or operate machinery when dizzy, unusually tired, weak or affected by nerve symptoms. Discuss adaptations and help with daily tasks.

items.title: General chemotherapy risks
items.text: Discuss low blood counts with serious infection or sepsis, anaemia and bleeding; nausea or vomiting; mouth soreness, appetite or taste changes, diarrhoea or constipation; fatigue, hair, nail and skin changes; changes in sexual wellbeing; allergic reactions and intravenous-line complications; blood clots, including clots in the legs or lungs; fertility, pregnancy and breastfeeding effects; and the possibility of lasting organ injury, rare later cancers or death from serious treatment complications. The likelihood and severity differ between medicines and people. Use this general discussion together with every medicine-specific risk below.

evidence.title: Eribulin versus dacarbazine: prespecified liposarcoma subgroup
evidence.summary: In the prespecified liposarcoma subgroup of a randomised trial, eribulin improved overall survival compared with dacarbazine. Participants had advanced dedifferentiated, myxoid/round-cell or pleomorphic liposarcoma and at least two previous systemic regimens.
evidence.intro: In the prespecified liposarcoma subgroup of a randomised trial, eribulin improved overall survival compared with dacarbazine. Participants had advanced dedifferentiated, myxoid/round-cell or pleomorphic liposarcoma and at least two previous systemic regimens.
evidence.caveat: Trial eligibility was narrower than the licensed indication. The result is not an individual prognosis and must not be generalised to leiomyosarcoma, all sarcomas or breast cancer. The trial salt dose is equivalent to the European base dose, not a higher prescribed base dose.
evidence.interpretation: Trial eligibility was narrower than the licensed indication. The result is not an individual prognosis and must not be generalised to leiomyosarcoma, all sarcomas or breast cancer. The trial salt dose is equivalent to the European base dose, not a higher prescribed base dose.

questions.q: What is the treatment trying to do?
questions.a: Eribulin aims to control liposarcoma and may help symptoms. Your consultant considers the precise subtype, prior treatment, fitness and what matters to you. A specialist sarcoma multidisciplinary team reviews the exact pathology, disease extent, prior treatment and your priorities. Surgery or radiotherapy can have a separate role in selected situations. Symptom control, rehabilitation and palliative care can accompany systemic treatment; they are not restricted to the end of life.

Eribulin 1.23 mg/m², expressed as eribulin base, is given on days 1 and 8 of each 21-day cycle. The team reviews safety before each dose. Treatment continues while benefit and tolerability justify it.

questions.q: Does a delay mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

questions.q: Who do I contact if unwell?
questions.a: Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.

questions.q: Can I restart after a delay or safety hold?
questions.a: Only after the treating team gives an explicit plan. A normal result does not erase a previous severe reaction or permanent-stop decision.

questions.q: Are safety tests the same as checking benefit?
questions.a: No. Safety tests look for treatment effects on the body. Scans, symptoms and function help the specialist assess tumour control.
